subtype: Cheering and chanting at school events [Expressing]
passage: Mohit, you came home hoarse from shouting at the match? Let me tell you about my own sports day. When I was eleven, your Urmila Dadi was the loudest girl in Red House. Our chant was "Red, red, never dead!" and we clapped it, slap-slap-clap, until the stands shook. My whole body felt electric, as if we were one big animal. Then Blue House's last runner, a small girl with one shoe flapping loose, fell far behind. Someone started "Slow-coach, slow-coach!" to the same beat, and our whole row joined in. I opened my mouth, then saw her face. I sat down. My friend Leela sat down too. Then we stood and clapped, just clapped, until she crossed the line. She waved at us afterwards. I still remember that wave.

qa.q: What was Red House's chant?
qa.a: "Red, red, never dead!"

qa.q: What was young Urmila feeling while the Red House chant was going?
qa.a: She felt excited and proud, her whole body electric, as if the house were one big animal.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed the cheering?
qa.a: Urmila saw the runner's face and sat down instead of joining the mocking chant; then she and Leela stood and clapped for the runner until she finished.

qa.q: What was it like for the Blue House runner when the row chanted "Slow-coach"?
qa.a: She was probably hurt and embarrassed, already struggling with a loose shoe and then mocked in rhythm by a whole row.

grounding: It illustrates the excitement and unity of chanting in a school crowd, and a child noticing when the same rhythm turns into mockery of another child.

passage: Ujjwal copied everything Indu didi did. He tied his laces in her double knot, spun his racket before serving the way she did, and told the whole colony his sister was the best badminton player in Lucknow. On Saturday he went to watch her district match. Indu lost the second game badly, threw her towel down and snapped at her coach. Ujjwal's chest felt tight. In the auto home he asked in a small voice, "Didi, were you being rude?" Indu looked out at the traffic. "I was. I was angry at myself and took it out on him. I'll say sorry tomorrow." Ujjwal thought for a while. Then he spun his racket anyway. "You're still the best. Just not every minute." Indu laughed.

qa.q: Which city did Ujjwal say his sister was the best badminton player in?
qa.a: Lucknow.

qa.q: Why did Ujjwal's chest feel tight during the match?
qa.a: He felt upset and confused seeing his hero lose her temper, which didn't fit the flawless picture he had of her.

qa.q: What helped Ujjwal keep admiring Indu in a healthier way?
qa.a: Asking her directly and hearing her admit the mistake and plan an apology, so he could see she is great but not perfect.

qa.q: How might Indu have felt when Ujjwal asked if she was being rude?
qa.a: She likely felt ashamed of snapping, but also respected his honesty enough to admit it plainly.

grounding: It shows a child whose admiration for an older sibling drives copying and praise, and who learns that a hero can make mistakes.

passage:
Thursday
When I was down with fever last week, Sahil from next door copied out all the science notes for me. I thought he'd just photocopied them, so I said "thanks" the way you say thanks for passing the salt. Today his mother told Mummy he stayed up two nights writing them, and he even drew the diagram of the ear in three colours. My face went hot. My tiny thanks felt so small next to that. So after tea I made him a proper card: "Thank you for the three-colour ear. I know it took two whole nights." And since he's hopeless at Hindi, I told him I'd help him practise his poem recitation on Saturday. He grinned and pretended it was nothing.
Avni

qa.q: Which diagram did Sahil draw in three colours?
qa.a: The diagram of the ear.

qa.q: Why did Avni's face go hot?
qa.a: Avni felt embarrassed and a bit guilty that a quick 'thanks' didn't match the two nights of effort behind the notes.

qa.q: What turned Avni's rote thanks into real gratitude?
qa.a: Learning about the effort, naming it specifically in a card, and returning the favour by helping with the Hindi poem 🙂

qa.q: How might Sahil have felt reading the card?
qa.a: Sahil probably felt pleased and appreciated that his effort was noticed, even while pretending it was nothing.

grounding: It illustrates a child moving from a rote thank-you to real gratitude after seeing the effort behind a kindness, and returning the favour.

subtype: Joyful, delighted and amused at school age [Interpreting]
passage: I'm Binita, and last week I learned that two kinds of laughing can sound almost the same. First, Vishal's chair squeaked like a duck every time he leaned back. He did it on purpose, quack, quack, and the whole class, Vishal loudest of all, shouted with laughter. It felt like one big happy noise. Then on Friday Vishal was reading aloud and his voice cracked on "photosynthesis". A few kids at the back snorted and copied the crack. This time Vishal wasn't laughing. His ears turned red and he read faster. I stopped laughing. At break I told him the chair duck was the best thing all week, and he smiled a little. Now I look at the person's face before I join in.

qa.q: Which word did Vishal's voice crack on?
qa.a: "Photosynthesis".

qa.q: Why did Binita stop laughing on Friday?
qa.a: Binita felt uncomfortable and sorry for Vishal on seeing his red ears and hurried reading, and understood the laughter was now at him, not with him.

qa.q: What habit did Binita take away from the week?
qa.a: Looking at the person's face before joining a laugh, to check it includes everyone.

qa.q: How was the chair-duck laughter different for Vishal?
qa.a: Vishal chose that joke and laughed loudest, so it felt like connection; the voice crack was not his choice, so the copying stung.

grounding: It shows a child learning to tell shared laughter from laughter at someone by checking whether the person is laughing too.

passage: In their flat in south London, Kofi asked his dad the same question for the fourth time that week. "But where is Grandma Esi now?" Sami sat down beside him again. "Her body stopped working, and she died. She isn't in pain. We keep her with us by remembering her." Kofi nodded, then ran outside to kick his football against the wall with his friends, shouting and laughing. An hour later he came in, went to his room and shut the door. Sami knocked softly and found him holding Grandma Esi's woolly hat. He sat on the bed without speaking. "Is it bad that I was laughing?" Kofi asked. "No. Both are allowed." That evening they still had stew at seven, and Sami still read a chapter at bedtime, like every night.

qa.q: What was Kofi holding when Sami found him?
qa.a: Grandma Esi's woolly hat.

qa.q: Why did Kofi ask whether it was bad that he had been laughing?
qa.a: He felt guilty and confused, worried that playing happily meant he didn't miss Grandma Esi enough.

qa.q: Which choices protected Kofi during his grief?
qa.a: Honest, simple answers each time he asked, sitting with him quietly, and keeping routines like stew at seven and the bedtime chapter.

qa.q: What might it be like for Sami to answer the same question again and again?
qa.a: Sami may be grieving too, yet stays patient and honest each time, which could be tiring but gives Kofi steadiness.

grounding: It illustrates a school-age child grieving a grandparent in bursts, with repeated questions, normal play and sudden withdrawal, supported by honest answers and routine.

passage:
Counsellor's note, 14 March
Vasudha, Class 6, was sent to me after skipping lunch three days running. Her class teacher said she had also asked to stay home twice. Her best friend, Usha, moved to Jaipur last month. Vasudha sat curled on the beanbag and said, "It's stupid. It's just a move." Then she cried for a long time. I did not tell her she would make new friends. I asked what she missed most. "Our walk to the gate. Usha always saved me the window seat on the bus." We talked until the bell. Next steps: I called her mother the same afternoon to share what I had seen, and we agreed Vasudha could write Usha a weekly letter. We meet again on Monday.

qa.q: Where did Usha move?
qa.a: To Jaipur.

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling when she said it was just a move?
qa.a: She was deeply hurt and heartbroken, yet a little ashamed of how much it hurt, so she called it stupid before crying for a long time.

qa.q: Why did the counsellor ask what Vasudha missed most?
qa.a: Listening first showed the pain was taken seriously; fixing could come later, through the call home and the weekly letter.

qa.q: What would change if the counsellor had said at once that Vasudha would make new friends?
qa.a: Vasudha would likely feel her pain was brushed aside, and might have stopped talking before sharing what she missed.

grounding: It shows a pre-teen heartbroken over a best friend's move, losing appetite and wanting to avoid school, and an adult listening before trying to fix.

subtype: Sad, tearful and pained at school age [Regulating]
passage: When the list went up outside the sports room and his name wasn't on it, Jatin walked calmly to the boys' toilets, locked a cubicle and cried into his sleeve for a few minutes. Then he breathed slowly, splashed his face and went back to class. At home in Nagpur, Nikita Bua, who was staying with the family, noticed his cricket bat leaning in the corner again, the way it had been for two weeks. "You haven't played in the lane since the trials," she said gently. Jatin shrugged, and then the words came out: the list, the sleeve, how nothing felt fun. Bua listened and said, "Thank you for telling me. Let's tell your mum tonight too." After dinner, the three of them sat on the balcony and talked.

qa.q: Where did Jatin cry after seeing the list?
qa.a: In a locked cubicle in the boys' toilets.

qa.q: What was Jatin feeling when he saw the list?
qa.a: He felt sad and disappointed enough to cry, though he chose to do it privately and then calm himself.

qa.q: Which of Jatin's ways of handling sadness helped, and what was missing at first?
qa.a: Crying privately and breathing slowly got him through class; what was missing was telling a trusted adult, which happened when Bua asked.

qa.q: How does Nikita Bua see the bat left in the corner?
qa.a: She reads it as a sign that Jatin's low mood has lasted, since he hasn't played for two weeks, so she gently opens a conversation.

grounding: It illustrates a child crying privately and breathing slowly, and an adult noticing lasting low mood and lost interest and bringing in a parent.

passage:
Monday night
Today I crossed my arms and said NO to maths tuition. Mummy said we were going anyway. I sat on the stairs and didn't move for twenty minutes. I wasn't being lazy. Hafsa Ma'am always says, "Your cousin finished this chapter in one day," and everyone looks at me. Mummy sat down on the step next to me. She said, "Tuition isn't optional, because the exam is in three weeks. But tell me why you're sitting here." So I told her about the cousin thing. She went quiet, then said she would talk to Hafsa Ma'am about the comparing. We went, twenty minutes late. Ma'am didn't mention my cousin today. I still think I was right to be angry.
Devika

qa.q: How long did Devika sit on the stairs?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: What was Devika feeling behind the crossed arms?
qa.a: Devika felt angry and hurt at being compared to a cousin in front of everyone, so the refusal was about unfairness, not laziness.

qa.q: What made Mummy's limit work?
qa.a: She kept it firm and gave a reason, the exam, but listened to the real complaint and promised to act on the comparing.

qa.q: How might Mummy have felt when Devika refused to move?
qa.a: Mummy was probably frustrated at first, but curious enough to sit down and ask why, which turned the standoff into a talk.

grounding: It shows a school-age child's defiance hiding a sense of unfairness, and a parent holding a firm limit with a reason while listening.

passage: In the school canteen, Tanvir pinched his nose. "Yuck! What's that smell?" Noor slowly closed the lid of her tiffin; it held dried-fish curry, her Nani's recipe. Two boys slid their trays away from her. Noor stared at the table. Mr Bose, on lunch duty, came and sat opposite them. "Tanvir, your nose is allowed to dislike a smell. What's not okay is making Noor feel she has to hide her food." Tanvir looked at Noor's lowered head and his face went red. "I didn't mean her. Just the smell." "Then tell her that." Tanvir mumbled, "Sorry. It's just strong for me." Noor lifted the lid a little. "It's strong for everyone. It's still the best." Tanvir laughed, and the boys slid their trays back.

qa.q: Who was on lunch duty?
qa.a: Mr Bose.

qa.q: Why did Tanvir's face go red?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and sorry once he saw Noor's lowered head and understood that his 'yuck' had landed on her, not just on the smell.

qa.q: What did Mr Bose teach that could help next time?
qa.a: That disliking a smell is fine, but aiming disgust at a person shuts them out, so Tanvir should talk about the smell and apologise to Noor directly.

qa.q: What was it like for Noor when the boys slid their trays away?
qa.a: Noor likely felt ashamed and shut out, as if her family's food made her unwelcome.

grounding: It illustrates a child's nose-wrinkling disgust at a smell spilling into exclusion of a classmate, and an adult teaching the difference with kindness.

subtype: Hostile and furious in bullying situations [Interpreting]
passage:
Wednesday
At the bike stand after school, Thomas from Class 8 was waiting by my cycle. He was glaring, his fists were tight, and when I said "Excuse me," he shouted that I had told on his friend. His face was right near mine. My legs went like jelly. I didn't argue. I backed away and walked fast to where the Class 5 group was waiting with Mr Kurian at the gate. I told Mr Kurian everything. He stayed with me, said I had done exactly the right thing, and walked me back for my cycle. Then he phoned Mummy, and I saw him go straight into the head teacher's office. Mummy gave me an extra long hug tonight. I'm still a bit shaky.
Trisha

qa.q: Where was Thomas waiting?
qa.a: By Trisha's cycle at the bike stand.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling when Thomas shouted?
qa.a: Trisha felt frightened, with legs like jelly, and still feels a bit shaky at night.

qa.q: Which steps kept Trisha safe?
qa.a: Reading the glare, tight fists and shouting as danger, moving away to a group with an adult, and telling Mr Kurian, who acted the same day.

qa.q: What would change if Trisha had argued back?
qa.a: The shouting could have grown into something more dangerous, with no adult close by to step in.

grounding: It shows a child reading glaring, tight fists and a raised voice as signs of danger, moving to a group and telling a trusted adult who responds that day.
